ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Participants of the LISS panel provided informed consent before participating in the study.
Importantly for the present study, in October 2010, LISS participants were invited to an assembled study called the Inter-personal effects of crying.
Most participants were married (60.4% or n = 2,383), while 25.3% have never been married (n = 997), 8.4% were divorced (n = 333), 5.4% were widowed (n = 214), and 0.5% were separated (n = 21).
Half of the participants were employed (51.2% or n = 2,021), 21.1% were retired (n = 833), 9.2% take care of the housekeeping (n = 363), and 7.8% attended school or are studying (n = 307).

The items were rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) and were averaged to yield a mean score for life 2 Within this assembled study, participants were randomly assigned to view and rate different emotions displayed in pictures and after that, randomly received items either about aggression or about social bonding prior to their empathy responses.
As in Study 1a, we included all well-being and health indicators that were measured after the completion of the empathy measure and used the same participant inclusion criteria.
Most participants were married (61.0% or n = 2,321), while 23.9% have never been married (n = 910), 9.0% were divorced (n = 343), 5.5% were widowed (n = 211), and 0.6% were separated (n = 21).

Half of the participants were (self-)employed workers (51.1% or n = 1,946), 21.7% were retired (n = 825), 9.5% take care of the housekeeping (n = 361), and 7.0% attend school or are studying (n = 268).
The sample consisted of N = 1,495 undergraduate students who completed the survey in exchange for partial course credit.
Participants were on average 19.6 years old (SD = 1.5, range = 18-43).
Participants were randomly assigned to see pictures of a specific emotion (i.e., neutral, happiness, anger, anxiety, sadness [with tears]).

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Participants of the LISS panel provided informed consent before participating in the study.

> Importantly for the present study, in October 2010, LISS participants were invited to an assembled study called the Inter-personal effects of crying.

> Most participants were married (60.4% or n = 2,383), while 25.3% have never been married (n = 997), 8.4% were divorced (n = 333), 5.4% were widowed (n = 214), and 0.5% were separated (n = 21).

> Half of the participants were employed (51.2% or n = 2,021), 21.1% were retired (n = 833), 9.2% take care of the housekeeping (n = 363), and 7.8% attended school or are studying (n = 307).

report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 3107 columns across 210 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 210 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants of the LISS panel provided informed consent before participating in the study.
Importantly for the present study, in October 2010, LISS participants were invited to an assembled study called the Inter-personal effects of crying.
Most participants were married (60.4% or n = 2,383), while 25.3% have never been married (n = 997), 8.4% were divorced (n = 333), 5.4% were widowed (n = 214), and 0.5% were separated (n = 21).
Half of the participants were employed (51.2% or n = 2,021), 21.1% were retired (n = 833), 9.2% take care of the housekeeping (n = 363), and 7.8% attended school or are studying (n = 307).

The items were rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) and were averaged to yield a mean score for life 2 Within this assembled study, participants were randomly assigned to view and rate different emotions displayed in pictures and after that, randomly received items either about aggression or about social bonding prior to their empathy responses.
As in Study 1a, we included all well-being and health indicators that were measured after the completion of the empathy measure and used the same participant inclusion criteria.
Most participants were married (61.0% or n = 2,321), while 23.9% have never been married (n = 910), 9.0% were divorced (n = 343), 5.5% were widowed (n = 211), and 0.6% were separated (n = 21).

Half of the participants were (self-)employed workers (51.1% or n = 1,946), 21.7% were retired (n = 825), 9.5% take care of the housekeeping (n = 361), and 7.0% attend school or are studying (n = 268).
The sample consisted of N = 1,495 undergraduate students who completed the survey in exchange for partial course credit.
Participants were on average 19.6 years old (SD = 1.5, range = 18-43).
Participants were randomly assigned to see pictures of a specific emotion (i.e., neutral, happiness, anger, anxiety, sadness [with tears]).
All tests were non-significant (all ps > .303) suggesting that empathy scores did not vary depending on whether participants were randomly assigned to one emotion or another.
Following the pictures, participants were randomly assigned to either receive questions on aggression or questions on social bonding.
Then all participants are asked about their relationship status, relationship duration, and whether they had been in a romantic relationship before.

During this submodule, participants were all presented with items about self-regulation (approach and avoidance; example item: "I am more focused on preventing loss than gaining profits.") and items about individualism vs. collectivism (example item: "My major goal in life is to achieve my ambitions.").

text.text: Research has been equivocal about whether empathy is associated with better or worse wellbeing and health.
Much of this research used cross-sectional samples to study a narrow range of well-being and health outcomes with a variety of different empathy scales, domains, and facets.

The present study examined whether two distinct facets of empathy-emotional empathy and cognitive empathy measured with the Basic Empathy Scale-were linked to average levels and trajectories of annually self-reported life satisfaction, general mood, happiness, mental health symptoms, physical health, and medical conditions across 9 years.

Using a large, representative sample of Dutch participants from the Longitudinal Internet studies for the Social Sciences (LISS; N = 3,948), growth curve models revealed that vicarious affect (i.e., emotional empathy) was associated with lower average levels of life satisfaction, general mood, and self-rated health and higher levels of mental health symptoms and medical conditions.
Little evidence emerged for emotional and cognitive empathy as consistent predictors of well-being and health trajectories.

Self-reporting accurate inference (i.e., cognitive empathy) was associated with reporting more medical conditions but was otherwise unrelated to well-being and health levels and trajectories (Study 1a).

Many of these results replicated with a different measure of emotional empathy (based on the Questionnaire Measure of Emotional Empathy; Study 1b [LISS; N = 3,806) and with an independent sample of young adults (Study 2; N = 1,495).
These findings provide impetus for further longitudinal research to clarify which specific facets of empathy play a role in predicting well-being and health over time.
Research on empathy can be characterized by two distinct perspectives.
On the one hand, empathy is regarded as positive and as a socially desirable characteristic that is valued by others (Ferguson et al., 2021).
text.formatted: On the one hand, empathy is regarded as positive and as a socially desirable characteristic that is valued by others <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Ferguson et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In that vein, empathy has been linked to a host of positive outcomes, such as support, happiness, and ostensibly prosocial moral behavior (e.g., Chopik et al., 2017; Hannikainen et al., 2020; Huo et al., 2019).

text.text: On the other hand, empathy has also been regarded as less favorable, having been associated with more negative outcomes, such as depressive symptoms, anxiety, and burnout (Yan et al., 2021).

text.text: This duality of empathy has also been discussed in recent popular psychology books, which either praise the value of empathy or argue against the benefits of empathy (Bloom, 2018; Krznaric, 2015).

text.text: Empathy's contradictive nature might partly stem from researchers using the term empathy in relation to a diverse set of empathy assessments that reflect different facets of empathy, which ultimately yield different associations with important life outcomes (Davis et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Empathy's contradictive nature might partly stem from researchers using the term empathy in relation to a diverse set of empathy assessments that reflect different facets of empathy, which ultimately yield different associations with important life outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Davis et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, a large portion of the studies linking empathy with important life outcomes, such as well-being and health, is built on cross-sectional data with specialized samples.
Therefore, despite extensive research on empathy, it remains unclear which facets of empathy are conducive to or harmful for people's well-being and health over time.

To address this ambiguity, the present study distinguishes two specific facets of empathy (i.e., emotional and cognitive empathy) as predictors of average levels and trajectories of health and well-being across nine years in a large representative Dutch sample.
Empathy has been defined in multiple ways (e.g., Cuff et al., 2016; Hall & Schwartz, 2019), and these definitions have emerged and evolved over time (Yan et al., 2021).

text.text: A recent definition of 15 empathy experts defines empathy as follows: "Empathy involves understanding, resonating with, and/or caring about others' experiences.
It encompasses the processes by which we come to experience or understand the internal states of others, as well as the judgments and affective responses that result." (Davis et al., 2026).

text.text: Although the structure and operationalization of empathy is heavily discussed, many researchers have adopted a twodimensional approach to understand and study empathy.
Broadly speaking, these two dimensions are comprised of an emotional/affective dimension and a cognitive/mental dimension-both including a variety of empathy facets.

In that recent consensus paper among 15 experts, various empathy facets were re-labeled to create a common lexicon to bring more clarity into what each empathy facet is measuring (Davis et al., 2026).

text.text: While some facets' original names have been labeled identically or very similarly, they have been measured with different instruments and are not identical in what they capture.
For the purposes of this study, we will retain the original labels of these facets and always refer to their assessment scale.

text.text: The cognitive/mental dimension of empathy also includes different facets to describe how individuals understand another person's feelings or thoughts.

One prominent facet of cognitive empathy which is measured with the BES (Jolliffe & Farrington, 2006) was originally labeled cognitive empathy and can be understood as self-rated inferential accuracy of others' feelings (Davis et al., 2026).

text.text: The expert consensus also concluded that perspective taking is an accurate description of this empathy facet.
The two facets correlate at between r = .33 to .37 with each other (Jolliffe & Farrington, 2006).

text.text: Although this was a conceptual clarification of empathy, it represents a promising way to organize empathy in ways that help adjudicate contradictory findings in past work and can potentially motivate formal factor analytic efforts to validate the framework.
Considering these emerging discussions, in describing the literature below, we mention which scales were used, as the lower-order facets are often yoked to a particular measure.

We also use the short-hand terms of emotional and cognitive empathy for the emotional and cognitive domains but contextualize our findings in view of the expert-consensus framework for our findings in the discussion.

Efforts for a consensus empathy framework are underway and look promising (e.g., Cuff et al., 2016; Davis et al., 2026; Eklund & Meranius, 2021), so explicitly contextualizing our results within these frameworks can provide a more precise understanding of how empathy might potentially affect health and well-being (Davis et al., 2026) foot_0.

text.text: Many facets of empathy are thought to be positively related to well-being and health because of their association with ostensibly positive inter-and intrapersonal constructs, which we label the salubrious-empathy pathway.

In particular, perspective taking, empathic concern, or the overall empathy score based on the IRI are linked to more emotional support receipt, larger support networks, and higher relationship quality (Huo et al., 2019; Kardos et al., 2017; Kimmes et al., 2014; Levesque et al., 2014).

text.text: Being emotionally reactive to partner stress is also linked to higher relationship quality in the short-and long-term among fledgling romantic couples (Selcuk et al., 2024).

text.text: Further, a meta-analysis found that pooled across different empathy measures, the emotional and cognitive empathy domains were negatively associated with criminal offending, although the effect for measures of the cognitive dimension was stronger compared to measures of the emotional dimension (Jolliffe & Farrington, 2004).

text.text: Empathic concern and perspective taking based on the IRI are also linked to ostensibly positive intrapersonal characteristics, such as agreeableness, conscientiousness, extraversion, self-esteem, and purpose in life (Coll et al., 2020; Manczak et al., 2016; Sommerlad et al., 2021).

text.text: In addition, individuals with higher levels of empathic concern (IRI) are more likely to use adaptive coping strategies.
These coping strategies likely provide opportunities to enhance or at least buoy their well-being in the context of stress (Prosek et al., 2022).
text.formatted: These coping strategies likely provide opportunities to enhance or at least buoy their well-being in the context of stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Prosek et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Further, given that empathy is one of the motivators for prosocial behavior, links between prosocial behavior and longevity could partially be initiated through empathic individuals' desires to help others and be altruistic (Konrath & Grynberg, 2016; Qu et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2025).

text.text: Furthermore, research suggests that healthcare providers' empathy (self-reported and perceived by patients) is linked to better health-outcomes in their patients (e.g., Dambha-Miller et al., 2019; Hojat et al., 2011; Lelorain et al., 2023; Licciardone et al., 2024), providing some evidence that being the recipient of empathy is linked to better physical health.

text.text: Furthermore, research from the COVID-19 pandemic showed that individuals higher in emotional empathy or who had empathy towards the most vulnerable were more likely to adhere to recommended health-protective behaviors (Lilleholt et al., 2024; Pfattheicher et al., 2020).

text.text: These inter-and intrapersonal correlates of empathy, in turn, are linked to higher well-being or health (Anglim et al., 2020; Cabras & Mondo, 2018; Kurnaz et al., 2020; Strickhouser et al., 2017), which might partly explain how and why empathy could be linked to higher well-being and health.

text.text: Empathy could, however, also be associated with lower well-being and health because of the potential burden and stress that accumulates from being empathic-a pathway we label the straining-empathy pathway.
Specifically, being emotionally empathic involves feeling others' pains and struggles, which can be very stressful (for a systematic review, see Nitschke & Bartz, 2023).
text.formatted: Specifically, being emotionally empathic involves feeling others' pains and struggles, which can be very stressful (for a systematic review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Nitschke & Bartz, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, empathic people provide more emotional and instrumental support and offer more advice to others (Huo et al., 2019), which can be taxing or even isolating over time.
text.formatted: In addition, empathic people provide more emotional and instrumental support and offer more advice to others <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Huo et al., 2019)</ref>, which can be taxing or even isolating over time.

text.text: This is consistent with the compassion-fatigue literature, which suggests that more compassionate professionals are at risk of experiencing lower well-being and health (Paiva-Salisbury & Schwanz, 2022).

text.text: People high in empathy are generally less emotionally stable (Sommerlad et al., 2021) and experience more perceived burden during stressful times, such as the COVID-19 pandemic (De Moor et al., 2022).

text.text: Being more emotionally unstable and facing more social demands could accumulate and be accompanied by lower well-being and health for empathic people (Anglim et al., 2020; Strickhouser et al., 2017).

text.text: In the following, we will review previous evidence regarding the positive and negative associations between empathy and well-being and health.

text.text: The reviewed studies measured well-being in terms of life satisfaction, happiness, or domain-specific life evaluations.
The picture of associations between measures of empathy and well-being measures mostly speak to a positive association, although occasionally non-significant associations emerged.
For both emotional and cognitive empathy, few gender differences were noted.
Thus, the salubrious-empathy pathway is corroborated by most studies.
We found no studies that suggested a negative association between empathy and well-being."

With regards to mental health, an earlier review article by Schreiter and colleagues (2013) has summarized 37 studies on the association between empathy and (sub)clinical depressive symptoms and concluded that empathic concern and lower cognitive empathy (e.g., perspective taking, empathic accuracy) were unrelated to subjective measures of depression.

text.text: In sum, cognitive empathy seems to be accompanied with better mental health, while most evidence suggests that emotional empathy measures are associated with more depression and anxiety.
In contrast, comparatively less research investigated the physical health correlates of the emotional and cognitive empathy domains.
One study with over 4,000 Finnish students, found that emotional empathy was associated with less favorable attitudes towards smoking and alcohol use (Kalliopuska, 1992).
text.formatted: One study with over 4,000 Finnish students, found that emotional empathy was associated with less favorable attitudes towards smoking and alcohol use <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Kalliopuska, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, another study found that higher state emotional empathy (1item measure) was associated with more alcoholic consumption on days when people drank, based on data of over 490 US adults.

Lastly, the study by Paro et al. (2014) found that perspective taking-a cognitive facet of empathy-was positively associated with self-rated health quality, while empathic concern was not associated with reports of the quality of physical health.
text.formatted: Lastly, the study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Paro et al. (2014)</ref> found that perspective taking-a cognitive facet of empathy-was positively associated with self-rated health quality, while empathic concern was not associated with reports of the quality of physical health.

text.text: As such, this reviewed body of research suggests that the emotional and cognitive empathy domains are linked to higher life satisfaction, and especially the cognitive dimension to better mental health, and potentially cognitive and emotional empathy in general to better physical health.
In addition, the existing body of research also suggests that especially emotional empathy might be a risk factor for lower mental health.
The salubrious-empathy and the straining-empathy pathways could also explain why empathy might predict changes in well-being and health over time.
Of course, empathy's positive associations with interpersonal outcomes, coping strategies, and health-protective behaviors might accumulate into stable or increasing well-being and health over time.
However, emotional empathy's associations with more taxing emotional and behavioral patterns might accumulate in decreasing well-being and health.
These hypothesized longitudinal effects assume that empathy is quite stable and captures a substantial portion of trait variance over time.

Previous studies show that empathy's rank-order stability coefficients are .48 across a 10-year measurement interval, .37 across a 20-year measurement interval (Oh et al., 2020), or even .79 across 12 years (Grühn et al., 2008), suggesting that empathy is moderately stable over time.
text.formatted: Previous studies show that empathy's rank-order stability coefficients are .48 across a 10-year measurement interval, .37 across a 20-year measurement interval <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Oh et al., 2020)</ref>, or even .79 across 12 years <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Grühn et al., 2008)</ref>, suggesting that empathy is moderately stable over time.

text.text: While these coefficients might vary as a function of the measure used or interval, we assume that empathy also contains a trait component, which might be associated with well-being and health over time.
While we examine the predictive validity of empathy for the levels and changes in wellbeing and health, we do not assume that empathy is the sole cause of these outcomes.
Other factors may influence empathy, well-being, and health (cf. Rohrer & Lucas, 2020), but we do not focus on them in the present study.

text.text: Moreover, previous research suggests that experiencing adversity might promote empathy, compassion, and altruism (e.g., Lim & DeSteno, 2016; Staub et al., 2008; but see Jayawickreme et al., 2021; Seery et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Moreover, previous research suggests that experiencing adversity might promote empathy, compassion, and altruism (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Lim & DeSteno, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Staub et al., 2008</ref>; but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Jayawickreme et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Seery et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In the context of our study, it is also plausible that living through challenging circumstances, mental health struggles, or physical illness might foster greater empathy for others.

Despite these different possible causal pathways, examining the long-term predictive validity of empathy is valuable for identifying individuals who may be at greater or lower risk of later declines in well-being and health.

We know of no longitudinal study that has employed a measure of cognitive and emotional empathy as predictors of life satisfaction, affective well-being, happiness, mental health, or physical health over time in the way the outcomes are operationalized here.

A related study, however, that examined cognitive and emotional empathy based on the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI; Davis, 1980) as predictors of caregivers' burden over 15 months found almost no significant longitudinal effects (van den Kieboom et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A related study, however, that examined cognitive and emotional empathy based on the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Davis, 1980)</ref> as predictors of caregivers' burden over 15 months found almost no significant longitudinal effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(van den Kieboom et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, the lack of sufficient knowledge of the longitudinal predictive validity of empathy for well-being and health provides an impetus for the present study.
The present research examines empathy as predictors of the levels and trajectories of well-being and health.

More specifically, with Study 1a we studied whether two empathy facets (i.e., emotional and cognitive empathy, as measured via the BES) were significant predictors of both average levels and trajectories of self-reported life satisfaction, affective well-being, happiness, mental health, self-rated health, and prevalence of medical conditions in a large sample followed across nine years (N = 3,974).
Then, with Study 1b, we used an almost identical sample (N = 3,804) but a different measure for emotional empathy to replicate the findings of Study 1a.

Lastly, Study 2 includes sensitivity analyses based on a convenience sample of young adults (N = 1,495) to check the robustness of the findings across different empathy measures and well-being and health outcomes.
We build on previous research in several ways.
First, this is one of the first projects that examined empathy as predictor of well-being and health trajectories across multiple years and over an extended time in individuals' lives.
The previously reviewed literature is mostly crosssectional and cannot make inferences about the predictive validity of empathy for long-term well-being and health developments.

Second, many of the reviewed studies on empathy and well-being and health have been conducted with specialized samples, such as healthcare professionals, (medical) students, adolescents, teachers, and caregivers (e.g., Bigdeli et al., 2021; Carrard et al., 2022; Dionigi et al., 2020; Hobeika et al., 2020; Hua et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2001; Lu et al., 2020; Paro et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).

text.text: The present study examined empathy in a nationally representative sample from the Netherlands to improve the generalizability of the associations between empathy and well-being and health.

Third, using a more holistic approach, we examined the effects of empathy by including both emotional and cognitive empathy (in addition to an overall composite of empathy to enable comparisons with past work) based on the BES as predictors of multiple well-being and health indicators (i.e., life satisfaction, general mood, happiness, mental health, self-rated health, medical conditions).

Furthermore, we conducted replication analyses with a similar sample based on emotional empathy measured with items of the QMEE and another large convenience sample of younger adults using items from the IRI.
These approaches enabled us to compare potentially different patterns of results across empathy facets and multiple outcomes.
With the present research, we hope to facilitate more generalizable claims about the role of emotional and cognitive empathy for well-being and health.
The goal of Study 1a was to examine the prediction of emotional and cognitive empathy on the levels and trajectories of a set of well-being and health indicators across a timespan of 9 years.

text.text: The LISS is a representative household panel from the Netherlands that has been collecting data since 2007.
The well-being and health variables are assessed annually since the beginning of the LISS (for exceptions, see the Measures section).
Importantly for the present study, in October 2010, LISS participants were invited to an assembled study called the Inter-personal effects of crying.
Part 1 of this assembled study included a set of questions regarding emotion recognition, aggression, social bonding, and empathy 2 .
This assembled study was sent to all LISS participants who were 16 years and older at the time (N = 7,428) and 71.9% (N = 5,339 respondents) completed it.

For this study, we used data from participants that provided information on empathy in 2010 and participated in at least three assessments of all well-being and health outcomes between 2011 and 2019 3 .
The final sample comprised of N = 3,948 participants who were on average 50.3 years old (SD = 16.7) at baseline with an age range from 16 to 90 years.
The gender distribution was 53.0% women (n = 2,092), and 47.0% male (n = 1,856).
Most participants were married (60.4% or n = 2,383), while 25.3% have never been married (n = 997), 8.4% were divorced (n = 333), 5.4% were widowed (n = 214), and 0.5% were separated (n = 21).
Half of the participants were employed (51.2% or n = 2,021), 21.1% were retired (n = 833), 9.2% take care of the housekeeping (n = 363), and 7.8% attended school or are studying (n = 307).
The remaining 10.7% of participants (n = 424) reported other employment categories, such as job seeking, (partial) work disability, or volunteer work.

text.text: Emotional and Cognitive Empathy.
Empathy was measured in October 2010 with the Basic Empathy Scale (BES).
The BES is a 20-item scale developed by Jolliffe and Farrington (2006).
text.formatted: The BES is a 20-item scale developed by <ref type="bibr">Jolliffe and Farrington (2006)</ref>.

text.text: The scale was designed with a two-factor structure (i.e., emotional and cognitive empathy).

Emotional empathy was measured with 11 items (e.g., "I get caught up in other people's feelings easily."); cognitive empathy was measured with 9 items (e.g., "I can usually work out when my friends are scared.").

The reliability of the overarching empathy scale (i.e., combining emotional and cognitive empathy) was w = .81, and for the two subscales, reliability was w = .77 for emotional empathy and w = .74 for cognitive empathy, respectively.
Recently, Carré and colleagues (2013) obtained a three-factor structure for the BES.
We also tested a three-factor structure but decided to use the original two-factor framework for our analyses due to the unreliability of the three-factor structure and item loadings.
The factor analytic results and more detailed argumentations for the usage of the original two-factor structure can be found in the Supplemental Material (Tables 18 19and Figure 3).
text.formatted: The factor analytic results and more detailed argumentations for the usage of the original two-factor structure can be found in the Supplemental Material (Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_7">18</ref> <ref type="table" target="#tab_8">19</ref>and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Life satisfaction was assessed annually (except in 2016) with the Satisfaction with Life Scale (Diener et al., 1985).
text.formatted: Life satisfaction was assessed annually (except in 2016) with the Satisfaction with Life Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Diener et al., 1985)</ref>.

Using the 1-7 scale below, indicate your agreement with each item by placing the appropriate number on the line preceding that item.
Please be open and honest in your responding."
An example item is: "The conditions of my life are excellent."

Because the measurement in 2010 preceded the assessment of empathy, we used the measurements of the years 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2017, 2018, and 2019 for this study.

text.text: Across these assessments, the reliabilities ranged from w = .91 to .94.
To capture affective well-being, we used two single items that measured general mood and happiness in the LISS.
As a measure of general mood, we used one item that was assessed annually (except in 2016).
The item asked, "In general, how do you feel?"
and was rated on a 7point Likert scale ranging from 1 (very bad) to 7 (very good).

Although single-item assessments provide less information about emotional experiences than multi-item measures (Dejonckheere et al., 2022), they can appropriately assess global affective valence and significantly reduce participant burden (Russell et al., 1989).
text.formatted: Although single-item assessments provide less information about emotional experiences than multi-item measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Dejonckheere et al., 2022)</ref>, they can appropriately assess global affective valence and significantly reduce participant burden <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">(Russell et al., 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Research has demonstrated the concurrent and predictive validity of single-item affect assessments in repeated-measures designs and of capturing enough variability relative to their multi-item counterparts (Kral et al., 2026; Song et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Research has demonstrated the concurrent and predictive validity of single-item affect assessments in repeated-measures designs and of capturing enough variability relative to their multi-item counterparts <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Kral et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Song et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Happiness.
As a measure of happiness, we used on item that was also assessed annually (except in 2016).
This happiness item asked participants, "On the whole, how happy would you say you are?"
and was rated on an 11-point scale ranging from 0 (totally unhappy) to 10 (totally happy).
Using single-item measures to assess happiness has been shown to be valid and reliable (Abdel-Khalek, 2006).
text.formatted: Using single-item measures to assess happiness has been shown to be valid and reliable <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abdel-Khalek, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Mental health symptoms were measured annually (except in 2014) with five items on a 6-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (never) to 6 (continuously).
These five items originated the Mental Health Index-5 (a variant of the measure developed by Ware & Sherbourne, 1992; see van der Velden et al. 2021).
text.formatted: These five items originated the Mental Health Index-5 (a variant of the measure developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">Ware & Sherbourne, 1992</ref>; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">van der Velden et al. 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The mental health index focused on depressive symptoms and anxiety.
The items were preceded with the statement: "The following questions are about how you felt over the past month.
For every question, please choose the answer that best describes how you felt during this past month.
This past month ....".
Example items include: "I felt very anxious" or "I felt depressed and gloomy".
Items were averaged, with higher scores indicating poorer mental health.
Across time points, reliabilities ranged from w =.88 to .91.
We used scores of mental health symptoms from the years 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2019 for this study.
text.formatted: We used scores of mental health symptoms from the years <ref type="bibr">2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2019</ref> for this study.

text.text: Self-Rated Health.
Self-rated health was measured annually (except in 2014) with a single-item measure that asked participants (Ware & Sherbourne, 1992): "How would you describe your health, generally speaking?"
text.formatted: Self-rated health was measured annually (except in 2014) with a single-item measure that asked participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Ware & Sherbourne, 1992)</ref>: "How would you describe your health, generally speaking?"

text.text: The statement was rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = poor,2 = moderate,3= good,4 = very good,5 = excellent).
We used the self-rated health scores from the years 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2019 for this study.
text.formatted: We used the self-rated health scores from the years <ref type="bibr">2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2019</ref> for this study.

text.text: In addition to self-rated health-a more subjective measure of health-we also included a sum score of different medical conditions to explore how farreaching the association between empathy and well-being and health is.
Medical conditions were assessed annually (except in 2014) with the following question: "Has a physician told you this last year that you suffer from one of the following diseases/problems?"
The participants answered this question with 18 items that included various medication conditions (e.g., heart attack, asthma, cancer).
We created a sum score across these items, with higher scores reflecting more medical conditions.
We used medical condition scores from the years 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2019 for this study.
text.formatted: We used medical condition scores from the years <ref type="bibr">2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2019</ref> for this study.

text.text: We conducted four sets of models.
We ran growth curve models for each well-being and health indicator separately with a structural equation approach (Bollen & Curran, 2006).
text.formatted: We ran growth curve models for each well-being and health indicator separately with a structural equation approach <ref type="bibr">(Bollen & Curran, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: One set of models estimated a linear slope for each indicator (6 models), and another set of models estimated an additional curvilinear (or quadratic) slope (6 models).
In the linear models, the repeated measures were specified as indicators of latent intercept and linear slope factors.

The intercept factor loadings were fixed to 1, while the loadings for the linear factor reflected the measurement intervals between assessments (which were not always equidistant) to reflect a linear slope.

These loadings were centered to the middle of the assessments so that the intercept can be interpreted as the average across the study (instead of as the level at the beginning of assessments, which was a random point in time for participants).
The loadings for the quadratic factor were squared to reflect a curvature trajectory.
Based on lower Akaike and Bayesian Information Criteria (AIC, BIC), we chose the model with the better relative fit.
We also considered changes in the CFI, RMSEA, and SRMR as indicative of better or worse model fit.

In a third set of models, we ran the previously determined best-fitting growth curve models with empathy (overall score) or its subscales (i.e., emotional empathy, cognitive empathy) as separate manifest predictors of the intercept (i.e., average level) and the slope of the respective well-being and health indicator (with no controls; number of models = 18).

In the fourth set of models, we ran these same models and included covariates (i.e., age, gender) to test the robustness of the findings (see Figure 1 for an illustration of one example model; number of models = 18).
text.formatted: In the fourth set of models, we ran these same models and included covariates (i.e., age, gender) to test the robustness of the findings (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> for an illustration of one example model; number of models = 18).

text.text: Control variables were allowed to covary with the empathy predictor and predicted the intercept and slope factors of the well-being and health indicators.

We chose separate models for each empathy predictor to make the results more comparable to the majority of previous studies that have employed separate models or bivariate (not partial) correlations (e.g., Bach et al., 2017; Carrard et al., 2022; Chopik et al., 2017; Lachmann et al., 2018; Paro et al., 2014).
text.formatted: We chose separate models for each empathy predictor to make the results more comparable to the majority of previous studies that have employed separate models or bivariate (not partial) correlations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bach et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Carrard et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Chopik et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Lachmann et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Paro et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Previous research has only combined the facets into one model when testing hierarchical regressions (e.g., Bennik et al., 2019; Coll et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2020); models that pursue a different goal than the current study.

text.text: In addition, empathy facets have been used as moderators in associations between different sets of variables, although not as moderators of each other (e.g., Oriol et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In addition, empathy facets have been used as moderators in associations between different sets of variables, although not as moderators of each other (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Oriol et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In fact, we are not aware of any literature that suggests that one facet moderates the association between the other facet and well-being and health.
Hence, we did not test moderation effects.
The growth curve models were conducted with a full information maximum likelihood (fiml) approach and a maximum likelihood estimation with robust standard errors (MLR).
To assess model fit, we used the comparative fit index (CFI), the root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and the Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR).
Model fit was deemed satisfactory when CFI ≥ .95, RMSEA ≤ .08, and SRMR ≤ .10 (Schermelleh-Engel et al., 2003).
For all models, time was centered, so the intercepts of each well-being and health indicator can be interpreted as average levels across time.

We computed 18 growth curve models, one for each empathy scale (i.e., empathy, emotional empathy, cognitive empathy; n = 3) and each well-being and health indicator (i.e.., life satisfaction, general mood, happiness, mental health symptoms, self-rated health, medical conditions; n = 6).
Based on a Bonferroni correction (0.05/18), we set the p-value to .003.
All predictors and outcome indicators were POMP/10 with the exception of gender.
Gender was coded0 = man,1 = woman.

The unstandardized regression coefficient b can be interpreted as the expected difference in the outcome associated with a 1-point higher score on the predictor (overall empathy, emotional empathy, or cognitive empathy), measured on the POMP/10 scale.
The standardized regression coefficient b indicates the expected difference, in standard deviations of the outcome, associated with a 1-SD difference in the predictor.
Note.
The factor loadings of the slope factors are adjusted to reflect the sometimes not equidistant assessment intervals (see Supplemental Material for more details).
Measurement Invariance.
We tested measurement invariance across time for the multiitem outcome scales (i.e., life satisfaction and mental health).
The results can be found in the Supplemental Tables 20 21.
text.formatted: The results can be found in the Supplemental Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_9">20</ref> <ref type="table" target="#tab_9">21</ref>.

text.text: The results of measurement invariance analyses supported scalar invariance across time.

However, because the model fit of these models was not satisfactory (despite model fit changes suggesting invariance), and because we want to run comparable models across all outcome scales (as some outcomes were based on single items and others on multiple items), we used the manifest mean scores as indicators for the analyses.

Means, standard deviations, and correlations between age, gender, empathy, emotional empathy, cognitive empathy, life satisfaction, general mood, and happiness are shown in Table 3 while the corresponding descriptive statistics for mental health, self-rated health, and medical conditions are shown in Table 4.

text.text: Initial correlations show that emotional empathy was negatively correlated with life satisfaction, general mood, and happiness across assessments.

Emotional empathy was positively correlated with mental health symptoms and negatively correlated with self-rated health across assessments; whereas cognitive empathy was positively correlated with medical conditions across assessments.

The intraclass correlations for life satisfaction (ICC = .70), general mood (ICC = .57), happiness (ICC = .62), mental health symptoms (ICC = .61), self-reported health (ICC = .65), and medical conditions (ICC = .82) across time suggest high between-person variance but also sufficient within-person variation to conduct growth curve models.
For all well-being and health indicators, the quadratic model was the model with the better relative fit based on a lower AIC and BIC (see Supplemental Table 22).

text.text: For transparency, we report both sets of models (without and with control variables) but focus on the models with control variables in the Discussion section.
Most effects of empathy on health and well-being were found for intercepts.

In the models without control variables, seven of 12 effects were significant (p < .003): Overall empathy was associated with lower average general mood (b = -.08, b = -0.10), higher average mental health symptoms (b = .20, b = 0.29), and lower average self-rated health (b = -.07, b = -0.13).
text.formatted: In the models without control variables, seven of 12 effects were significant (p < .003): Overall empathy was associated with lower average general mood (b = -.08, b = -0.10), higher average mental health symptoms (b = .20, b = 0.29), and lower average self-rated health (b = -.07, b = -0.13).

text.text: These effects, however, were driven by effects of emotional empathy.

Emotional empathy was associated with lower average life satisfaction (b = -0.05, b = -0.08) and general mood (b = -.11, b = -0.12), and with higher average mental health symptoms (b = .24, b = 0.28) and lower average self-rated health (b = -.08, b = -0.11).
Cognitive empathy was only significantly associated with higher average medical conditions (b = .06, b = 0.05).
The results with the models that controlled for age and gender found almost identical results.

Ten of 12 effects were significant in these adjusted models: The only difference to the unadjusted results of Table 6 is that, after controlling for age and gender, overall and emotional empathy also emerged as a significant predictor of more average medical conditions (overall empathy: b = .08, b = 0.06; emotional empathy: b = .05, b = 0.04, see Table 7).
text.formatted: Ten of 12 effects were significant in these adjusted models: The only difference to the unadjusted results of Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_5">6</ref> is that, after controlling for age and gender, overall and emotional empathy also emerged as a significant predictor of more average medical conditions (overall empathy: b = .08, b = 0.06; emotional empathy: b = .05, b = 0.04, see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_6">7</ref>).

text.text: Overall, the unadjusted and adjusted models generally provided similar results.
Specifically, emotional empathy in particular was associated with worse well-being and health, on average.
In predicting changes (i.e., slopes) in the six well-being and health indicators, there were only two significant effects (p < .003).
text.formatted: In predicting changes (i.e., slopes) in the six well-being and health indicators, there were only two significant effects (p < .003).

text.text: Specifically, overall and emotional empathy were negatively associated with the linear slope of mental health symptoms (b = -.10 or -.09, bs = -0.01).
In other words, people who scored 1 point higher in emotional empathy experienced on average a steeper decline (-0.01 points per year) in mental health symptoms over time.
No significant associations were found for the quadratic slopes (see Table 6).
text.formatted: No significant associations were found for the quadratic slopes (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_5">6</ref>).

text.text: When controlling for age and gender (see Table 7), the slope effects did not reach significance on a p < .003 level.
text.formatted: When controlling for age and gender (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_6">7</ref>), the slope effects did not reach significance on a p < .003 level.

text.text: Overall, the results between the unadjusted and adjusted models suggest that emotional and cognitive empathy were largely unrelated to how well-being and health indicators changed over time.
We also explored whether the regression coefficients between empathy and well-being and health indicators differ between women and men.

For that purpose, we ran multi-group analyses and set the three coefficients of interest to be equal across gender groups (i.e., women, men) and compared them to models where these coefficients could freely vary between women and men.
The results of those model comparisons are reported in Supplemental Table 24 and suggest no gender differences in these effects.

The goal of Study 1b was to test whether the results of Study 1a replicate with a broader emotional empathy measure that measures multiple empathy facets at once (Davis et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The goal of Study 1b was to test whether the results of Study 1a replicate with a broader emotional empathy measure that measures multiple empathy facets at once <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Davis et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For that purpose, we conducted analyses with a second empathy measure originating from a different assembled study of the LISS panel.
As in Study 1a, we included all well-being and health indicators that were measured after the completion of the empathy measure and used the same participant inclusion criteria.
The sample for these replication analyses consists of N = 3,806 participants.
Of those participants, n = 3,527 overlapped with the sample of Study 1a (89.3%).
The sample of Study 1b was on average 51.2 years old (SD = 16.4) with an age range from 16 to 90 years.
The gender distribution was 53.2% women (n = 2,024), and 46.8% men (n = 1,782).
Most participants were married (61.0% or n = 2,321), while 23.9% have never been married (n = 910), 9.0% were divorced (n = 343), 5.5% were widowed (n = 211), and 0.6% were separated (n = 21).

Half of the participants were (self-)employed workers (51.1% or n = 1,946), 21.7% were retired (n = 825), 9.5% take care of the housekeeping (n = 361), and 7.0% attend school or are studying (n = 268).
The remaining 10.7% of participants reported other employment categories, such as job seeking, (partial) work disability, or volunteer work.

In February 2011, 4 months after the BES assessment, another assembled study called Self-Regulatory Orientation: Addressing a basic aspect of the self and its relation to social indicators and life-outcomes and was sent out to all LISS participants 16 years and older (N = 7,155) of which 71.4% (N = 5,093) completed the study.
This submodule contained a measure of emotional empathy that is based on the Questionnaire Measure of Emotional Empathy (QMEE; Mehrabian & Epstein, 1972), which originally included 33 items.
text.formatted: This submodule contained a measure of emotional empathy that is based on the Questionnaire Measure of Emotional Empathy (QMEE; <ref type="bibr">Mehrabian & Epstein, 1972)</ref>, which originally included 33 items.

text.text: The assembled study of the LISS used 8 of these 33 items to measure emotional empathy (see Supplemental Table 2 for all items) 5 .
text.formatted: The assembled study of the LISS used 8 of these 33 items to measure emotional empathy (see Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> for all items) <ref type="foot" target="#foot_2">5</ref> .

text.text: Example items included "I get very angry when I see someone being ill-treated" or "I become nervous if others around me seem to be nervous."
These items were rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (totally not applicable) to 7 (totally applicable).
The Omega reliability of this emotional empathy measure was w = .91.
To check how the emotional empathy scale of the QMEE statistically overlaps with the BES-A, we computed correlations based on a sample of N = 3,548 participants, who responded to both scales.
The emotional empathy scale based on the QMEE was positively correlated with overall empathy (BES; r = .45), emotional empathy (BES-A; r = .45), and cognitive empathy (BES; r = .27).

We used the same well-being and health measures and assessment waves as reported in the main manuscript, except for the first 2010 assessments of mental health symptoms, self-rated health, and medical conditions, which were prior to the QMEE assessment.
The reliabilities of life satisfaction (w = .91 and .94) and mental health symptoms (w = .89 and .91) were comparable to those of the main sample.
The same models were run as in Study 1a but we included emotional empathy (based on the QMEE items) as predictor of levels and slopes of well-being and health indicators over time.

text.text: Similar to the main findings, emotional empathy measured based on the QMEE predicted lower life satisfaction and self-rated health and more mental health symptoms and medical conditions, on average.
Unlike the main findings, no significant prediction effects were found for well-being and health trajectories over time.
Thus, across these two measures, the effects of average levels seem replicable, while the effects on well-being and health trajectories are less robust.

We found that emotional empathy was significantly associated with lower levels of life satisfaction (b = -.10, b = -0.09), lower levels of general mood (b = -.12, b = -0.08), lower levels of happiness (b = -.08, b = -0.04), more mental health symptoms (b = .26, b = 0.19), lower levels of self-rated health (b = -.19, b = -0.16), and more medical conditions (b = .16, b = 0.07), on average.

text.text: Study 2: Sensitivity Analyses The consistent negative associations that we obtained between emotional empathy and well-being in Studies 1a and 1b contradict a large body of research showing positive associations between emotional empathy and well-being (Chopik et al., 2017; Coll et al., 2020; Lachmann et al., 2018; Oriol et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Study 2: Sensitivity Analyses The consistent negative associations that we obtained between emotional empathy and well-being in Studies 1a and 1b contradict a large body of research showing positive associations between emotional empathy and well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chopik et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Coll et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Lachmann et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Oriol et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, we conducted a correlational study among US college undergraduates (N = 1,495) to examine not only BES empathy's associations with well-being and health but also its overlap with the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI) and a single-item measure of empathy.

To gain a deeper understanding of empathy's correlates, we also included other characteristics in empathy's nomological network (i.e., Big Five domains, narcissism, optimism, positive and negative affect, purpose in life) together with some of the well-being and health indices of Studies 1a and 1b [medical conditions were not assessed given their low prevalence in young adults]).
The sample consisted of N = 1,495 undergraduate students who completed the survey in exchange for partial course credit.
Participants were on average 19.6 years old (SD = 1.5, range = 18-43).
The majority reported being women (61.2%), followed by men (38.4%), and 0.4% identified as other.

Participants' race/ethnicity was constituted as follows: 70.9% White, 11.6% Asian, 5.6% Black/African American, 3.4% Latinx, 4.9% multiracial, 2.7% other, 0.5% American Indian/Alaskan Native, 0.3% don't know/not sure, and 0.2% Native Hawaiian/other Pacific Islander.
As in Study 1a, empathy was measured with the Basic Empathy Scale (Jolliffe & Farrington, 2006).

text.text: Partially replicating our results in the longitudinal LISS sample, emotional empathy (BES) was associated with more mental health symptoms (r = .21) and worse self-rated health (r = -.10) but only negligibly associated with life satisfaction (r = .02).

Despite the high correlation with empathic concern (IRI), the results differed: empathic concern (IRI) was associated with higher life satisfaction (r = .12) but also more mental health symptoms (r = .09) and negligibly with self-rated health (r = -.003).
Thus, this smaller, cross-sectional study of US college students also confirmed that emotional empathy (BES) was associated with worse well-being and health.

The present research examined emotional and cognitive empathy facets as predictors of well-being and health levels and trajectories over a period of nine years.

Despite a larger body of evidence that suggests empathy being associated with better well-being and health outcomes, we found that, in Study 1a, people higher in emotional empathy (or vicarious affect) experienced lower well-being and health, on average.
We found little evidence that emotional or cognitive empathy may buffer the declines in well-being and health over time.

Furthermore, in Study 1b based on a different emotional empathy measure, we largely replicated that emotional empathy (QMEE items) was associated with worse well-being and health, on average,-which also partly replicated in Study 2.
In contrast, empathic concern (IRI; also labeled sympathy/compassion) another traditional measure of emotional empathy was more positively associated with well-being and health.

Relating these findings to a recent expert-consensus taxonomy (Davis et al., 2026), our findings suggest that the emotional empathy facet that describes individuals who are likely to feel what others are feeling (also labeled vicarious affect; Davis et al., 2026) is linked to lower well-being and health, while compassion and sympathy might be associated with more positive wellbeing and health outcomes.
text.formatted: Relating these findings to a recent expert-consensus taxonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Davis et al., 2026)</ref>, our findings suggest that the emotional empathy facet that describes individuals who are likely to feel what others are feeling (also labeled vicarious affect; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Davis et al., 2026)</ref> is linked to lower well-being and health, while compassion and sympathy might be associated with more positive wellbeing and health outcomes.

text.text: The cognitive empathy facet that describes individuals who are likely to report being correct in picking up on others' emotions (also labeled selfreported accurate inference; Davis et al., 2026) was largely unrelated to well-being and health across Studies 1a and 1b, but positively associated with well-being and health in Study 2.
text.formatted: The cognitive empathy facet that describes individuals who are likely to report being correct in picking up on others' emotions (also labeled selfreported accurate inference; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Davis et al., 2026)</ref> was largely unrelated to well-being and health across Studies 1a and 1b, but positively associated with well-being and health in Study 2.

text.text: We want to highlight that these effects are generally very small to small (|bs| ranging from .05 to .26).
Except for mental health symptoms and purpose (Study 2), which had small to medium effects, all other effects with well-being and health indicators were very small.
Different theoretical reasons could be adduced to explain why higher emotional empathy (i.e., vicarious affect or the QMEE items) was linked to lower well-being and health in this study.

First, in line with the straining-empathy pathway, emotional empathy might result in lower well-being and health through the psychological strain of taking on and experiencing other people's emotions and perspectives.

Specifically, feeling with, taking on the negative emotions of, and then potentially caring for other people can be emotionally and physically draining (e.g., Li et al., 2025; Paiva-Salisbury & Schwanz, 2022).
text.formatted: Specifically, feeling with, taking on the negative emotions of, and then potentially caring for other people can be emotionally and physically draining (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Li et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Paiva-Salisbury & Schwanz, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: And thus, being emotionally empathic could translate to worse wellbeing and health because of the emotional cost of empathizing and the accompanying physical health consequences of that added emotional distress.

This is consistent with previous findings linking emotional empathy-and especially contagion but not compassion/sympathy-to more mental health symptoms and burnout (for metaanalyses, see Delgado et al., 2023; Martingano et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This is consistent with previous findings linking emotional empathy-and especially contagion but not compassion/sympathy-to more mental health symptoms and burnout (for metaanalyses, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Delgado et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Martingano et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">Yan et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, agreeableness-one of the Big Five traits-was moderately associated with all facets of empathy (see Study 2, and Supplemental Tables 31 and 32 for associations in Study 1a and 1b).
text.formatted: Interestingly, agreeableness-one of the Big Five traits-was moderately associated with all facets of empathy (see Study 2, and Supplemental Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">31</ref> and <ref type="table" target="#tab_9">32</ref> for associations in Study 1a and 1b).

text.text: In contrast to our findings with emotional empathy, however, agreeableness is typically associated with positive well-being and health behaviors (for meta-analyses, see Anglim et al., 2020; Pletzer et al., 2024; Strickhouser et al., 2017).

text.text: The facets related to emotional empathy (BES' emotional empathy and IRI's empathic concern), however, were more strongly linked to the Big Five trait of neuroticism (or negative emotionality) compared to the cognitive empathy facets of the BES and the IRI; a Big Five trait traditionally linked to lower well-being and health (e.g., Anglim et al., 2020; Pletzer et al., 2024; Strickhouser et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The facets related to emotional empathy (BES' emotional empathy and IRI's empathic concern), however, were more strongly linked to the Big Five trait of neuroticism (or negative emotionality) compared to the cognitive empathy facets of the BES and the IRI; a Big Five trait traditionally linked to lower well-being and health (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Anglim et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Pletzer et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Strickhouser et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, vicariously feeling for someone (BES emotional empathy) or being sympathetic and compassionate (IRI empathic concern) might require emotional variability or reactivity (Mader et al., 2023) to other people's emotions.
text.formatted: Hence, vicariously feeling for someone (BES emotional empathy) or being sympathetic and compassionate (IRI empathic concern) might require emotional variability or reactivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Mader et al., 2023)</ref> to other people's emotions.

text.text: Hence, teasing apart why emotional empathy is social (i.e., agreeable) and stressful (i.e., neurotic) at the same time might elucidate the inconsistent associations with well-being and health.
Second, an empathic response might be more readily provided by people who are experiencing difficult times themselves, such as facing lower well-being and worse mental and physical health.

People who are less happy and who experience mental or physical health challenges might be more receptive to the negative emotions of others given that they so intimately know them themselves (Hill et al., 2010; van Hoven & Perrone-McGovern, 2019).
text.formatted: People who are less happy and who experience mental or physical health challenges might be more receptive to the negative emotions of others given that they so intimately know them themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Hill et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">van Hoven & Perrone-McGovern, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In fact, findings from fMRI studies established that the neurological pathways for experiencing pain are often shared with those activated when experiencing empathy and other social emotional characteristics (Fallon et al., 2020; Kross et al., 2011; Lamm et al., 2011).
text.formatted: In fact, findings from fMRI studies established that the neurological pathways for experiencing pain are often shared with those activated when experiencing empathy and other social emotional characteristics <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Fallon et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Kross et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Lamm et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: This makes it likely that individuals who are experiencing painful experiences-potentially linked to their lower well-being and health-could more readily empathize with others.

Given that empathy and pain share neural circuitry, and that empathy recruits neural networks involved in the first-hand experience of pain, it could be that those with more painful life experiences have more well-potentiated pathways, and as such higher capacity for concurrent emotional empathy.
Future research should more deliberately examine this preliminary idea.

Third, a more methodological reason for the contradiction with some literature is that our measures (i.e., BES, QMEE) differed from previous studies that found wellbeing and health benefits for measures of the emotional and cognitive domains of empathy (Coll et al., 2020; Oriol et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Third, a more methodological reason for the contradiction with some literature is that our measures (i.e., BES, QMEE) differed from previous studies that found wellbeing and health benefits for measures of the emotional and cognitive domains of empathy <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Coll et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Oriol et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: But our findings are consistent with previous findings that used other empathy measures (i.e., not BES or IRI), a conglomerate across measures, adapted versions of the IRI and QMEE, or an overall empathy score based on the IRI (Carrard et al., 2022; Hua et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2023; Manczak et al., 2016).
text.formatted: But our findings are consistent with previous findings that used other empathy measures (i.e., not BES or IRI), a conglomerate across measures, adapted versions of the IRI and QMEE, or an overall empathy score based on the IRI <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Carrard et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Hua et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Kumar et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Manczak et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, our findings do not converge with findings largely based on the IRI, pointing to a positive link between empathic concern and higher subjective well-being and better mental health (Chopik et al., 2017; Chung et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2020; Paro et al., 2014).
text.formatted: In addition, our findings do not converge with findings largely based on the IRI, pointing to a positive link between empathic concern and higher subjective well-being and better mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chopik et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chung et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Huang et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Paro et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In our student sample, while highly correlated, emotional empathy (BES) and empathic concern (IRI) are sometimes similarly and sometimes dissimilarly related to well-being and health indicators.
The current body of research enriched with findings of the present study cannot yet paint a clear picture about the role of empathy for well-being and health-especially in the long-term.

However, recent evidence shows that interventions to increase positive empathy-being empathic for the positive feelings of others-does increase affective and cognitive well-being (Depow et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, recent evidence shows that interventions to increase positive empathy-being empathic for the positive feelings of others-does increase affective and cognitive well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Depow et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, future studies might focus on the content of the emotions that participants empathize with.
Lastly, it is likely that emotional empathy is not the causal factor behind lower well-being and health levels.
While we controlled for age and gender, other potential variables have not been considered.
Such third variables could be the cause of higher emotional empathy and lower well-being and health.

Plausible candidate factors could be adversity and traumatic experiences, which have partly been shown to be linked to worse well-being and health but also higher empathy and compassion (e.g., Kalmakis et al., 2015; Lim & DeSteno, 2016; Sahle et al., 2022; Staub et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Plausible candidate factors could be adversity and traumatic experiences, which have partly been shown to be linked to worse well-being and health but also higher empathy and compassion (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Kalmakis et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Lim & DeSteno, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Sahle et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Staub et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, it can be a goal of a different study to test whether other constructs act as moderators in the association between emotional and cognitive empathy, and well-being and health to provide more context regarding the boundary conditions for associations between empathy, well-being, and health.
We can only speculate on the reasons for the lack of associations between empathy and the trajectories of well-being and health in the present study.

First, while a previous study testing emotional and cognitive empathy as predictors of caregivers' burden over 15 months also found almost no longitudinal effects (van den Kieboom et al., 2023), it is possible that empathy might predict shorter-term changes in well-being and health and not across longer periods.
text.formatted: First, while a previous study testing emotional and cognitive empathy as predictors of caregivers' burden over 15 months also found almost no longitudinal effects (van den <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Kieboom et al., 2023)</ref>, it is possible that empathy might predict shorter-term changes in well-being and health and not across longer periods.

text.text: Previous research has shown moderate to high stability-but also changes-in empathy across the lifespan (Grühn et al., 2008; Oh et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Previous research has shown moderate to high stability-but also changes-in empathy across the lifespan <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Grühn et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Oh et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, empathy might be undergoing its own changes while people's wellbeing and health also change.
With only one assessment of empathy being used to predict health and well-being changes across a decade, the predictive power of empathy might be reduced.
Repeated measures of empathy would have been useful in specifying the time course and direction of the empathy-outcome associations.
Thus, shorter intervals or models that capture the reciprocal links between empathy and well-being and health over time could be better suited to detect longitudinal effects (Yang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Thus, shorter intervals or models that capture the reciprocal links between empathy and well-being and health over time could be better suited to detect longitudinal effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">(Yang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Another potential reason for the lack of longitudinal prediction is that empathy might not predict changes in well-being and health but rather in more context-specific variables-such as relationship outcomes.

For example, a study with over 1,500 participants showed that levels and changes in empathy in adolescence predicted social outcomes, such as communication skills and social integration at the age of 35 years old (Allemand et al., 2015).
text.formatted: For example, a study with over 1,500 participants showed that levels and changes in empathy in adolescence predicted social outcomes, such as communication skills and social integration at the age of 35 years old <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allemand et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The translation between the longitudinal effects of empathy on social relationships to general well-being and health indicators might be more complex and thus not directly detectable in a longitudinal association between empathy and wellbeing and health.

The present study extends previous research by using a larger, more representative sample and longitudinal data to provide initial evidence of the links between emotional and cognitive empathy and well-being and health by testing two empathy facets.
This study is among one the largest and longest studies examining the well-being and health outcomes of empathy conducted to date.
The consistency of the negative associations between emotional empathy and lower well-being and health underscores the robustness of that link.
Furthermore, we collected cross-sectional data to replicate the effects for the BES and to link them with the more widely used IRI.
Despite the strengths of the present study, some limitations need to be highlighted.
First, a larger battery of empathy measures is needed to understand the link between empathy and well-being and health.

The expert consensus by Davis and colleagues (2026) also labels the facets of the Adolescent Measure of Empathy and Sympathy (Vossen et al., 2015) as self-reported accurate inference, vicarious affect, and sympathy/compassion-similar to the two facets of the BES and the emotional facet of the IRI.
text.formatted: The expert consensus by <ref type="bibr">Davis and colleagues (2026)</ref> also labels the facets of the Adolescent Measure of Empathy and Sympathy <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">(Vossen et al., 2015)</ref> as self-reported accurate inference, vicarious affect, and sympathy/compassion-similar to the two facets of the BES and the emotional facet of the IRI.

text.text: Thus, replicating our findings with measures that experts deem overlapping would be a promising replication attempt.
Furthermore, such heterogeneity could also be further investigated on the item level of each empathy measure.

For the BES and the QMEE-based items in the present study, we found that some items more consistently mirrored the mean-score based associations with the well-being and health indicators, compared to others (see Supplemental Tables 33 and 34).
