text.text: Our findings also need to be cross-validated with empathy measures that are not self-reported, such as behavioral or neurocognitive measures (Neumann, 2015).
text.formatted: Our findings also need to be cross-validated with empathy measures that are not self-reported, such as behavioral or neurocognitive measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Neumann, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This is particularly important because selfreported empathy does not always translate into prosocial behaviors, motivations, or abilities (e.g., Underwood & Moore, 1982; Eisenberg & Miller, 1987; Murphy & Lilienfield, 2019), shows stronger gender differences than more objective measures (e.g., Eisenberg & Lennon, 1983; Pang et al., 2013), and is subject to socially desirable responding and impression management (Sassenrath, 2020).
text.formatted: This is particularly important because selfreported empathy does not always translate into prosocial behaviors, motivations, or abilities (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Underwood & Moore, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Eisenberg & Miller, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Murphy & Lilienfield, 2019)</ref>, shows stronger gender differences than more objective measures (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Eisenberg & Lennon, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pang et al., 2013)</ref>, and is subject to socially desirable responding and impression management (Sassenrath, 2020).

text.text: These caveats need to be kept in mind when interpreting the present findings.
Second, as mentioned previously, empathy was only measured once.
We did not have data about how the participants' empathy changed across the following decade and how there might be reciprocal effects with well-being and health over time.
Along these lines, a previous study showed that day-to-day empathy was higher when participants experienced both positive and negative affect and social events (Nezlek et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Along these lines, a previous study showed that day-to-day empathy was higher when participants experienced both positive and negative affect and social events <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Nezlek et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, future studies could promote knowledge into the reasons and mechanisms behind the associations between lower well-being and health and higher emotional empathy.
Finally, while using a representative sample was a strength of the study, it is possible that the associations between empathy and well-being and health are different across cultures.
The literature review was based on samples from some countries across the globe, which could also have been another factor contributing to the inconsistent findings.
Learning more about the cultural differences in the expression and correlates of emotional and cognitive empathy would be insightful in this context.

In addition, it would be valuable to examine empathy in those at risk for lower well-being and health, such as members of the racially/ethnically, gender, or sexually minoritized groups (e.g., Mandracchia et al., 2023) to understand whether empathy is a protective or risk factor for well-being and health in marginalized groups.
text.formatted: In addition, it would be valuable to examine empathy in those at risk for lower well-being and health, such as members of the racially/ethnically, gender, or sexually minoritized groups (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Mandracchia et al., 2023)</ref> to understand whether empathy is a protective or risk factor for well-being and health in marginalized groups.

text.text: While there is evidence demonstrating that emotional and cognitive empathy is positively associated with well-being and health, this longitudinal analysis based on a representative Dutch sample suggests that emotional empathy in particular is linked to lower average well-being and health.
There was little evidence showing empathy was protective for health and well-being changes across time.
More longitudinal studies and explicit tests of the mechanisms linking empathy to well-being and health are needed to understand the long-term predictive value of empathy for people's lives.
The Interpersonal Effects of Crying submodule consisted of two parts.
Empathy was measured in the first part in October 2010.
Participants first responded to the following question: "How long has it been since the last time you cried?", then they were shown pictures of faces.
Participants were randomly assigned to see pictures of a specific emotion (i.e., neutral, happiness, anger, anxiety, sadness [with tears]).
Then they were asked to rate the person in the picture (i.e., happy, sad, angry, attractive, nice).
We ran ANOVAs across the emotion conditions (neutral, happiness, anger, anxiety, sadness [with tears]) for the overall empathy, the emotional empathy, and the cognitive empathy score.
All tests were non-significant (all ps > .303) suggesting that empathy scores did not vary depending on whether participants were randomly assigned to one emotion or another.
text.formatted: All tests were non-significant (all ps > .303) suggesting that empathy scores did not vary depending on whether participants were randomly assigned to one emotion or another.

text.text: Following the pictures, participants were randomly assigned to either receive questions on aggression or questions on social bonding.

Questions on aggression were about creating words from random letters, reading and rating a scenario about someone who conducted money fraud and rating what punishment they should receive, and answering three items about anger and aggression.
The questions on social bonding were about donating money, social connection with the inclusion of the other in the self-scale, and rating three items about the need to belong.
Then all participants are asked about their relationship status, relationship duration, and whether they had been in a romantic relationship before.
Those participants who had been in a relationship before were also asked about the relationship duration of their longest relationship and presented with items about their romantic attachment style.
After that battery of questions and randomized conditions, the BES empathy questions were presented.

We ran independent sample t-tests for the two experimental conditions (either aggression or social bonding questions) and there were no significant differences in the overall empathy, emotional empathy, or cognitive empathy scores (all ps > .736).
text.formatted: We ran independent sample t-tests for the two experimental conditions (either aggression or social bonding questions) and there were no significant differences in the overall empathy, emotional empathy, or cognitive empathy scores (all ps > .736).

text.text: Hence, which conditions they were exposed to prior to filling out the Basic Empathy Scale did not predict their scores.

Factor Analysis To examine whether the full-scale empathy latent factor is feasible with our sample and to examine the subscale structure of the BES, we ran three confirmatory factor analyses.
First, we examined the one-factor structure of the BES including all items.
This was to examine whether it would be possible to include an overarching latent empathy factor into our analyses.
The model fit was unsatisfactory (CFI = .490, RMSEA = .104, SRMR = .101).
As mentioned, the scale was designed on the basis of a two-factor structure (Jolliffe & Farrington, 2006).
text.formatted: As mentioned, the scale was designed on the basis of a two-factor structure <ref type="bibr">(Jolliffe & Farrington, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, in a second step, we included a two-factor structure with items either loading unto an emotional or cognitive empathy factor.
Both latent factors were correlated.
The model fit improved slightly but remained unsatisfactory (CFI = .641, RMSEA = .087, SRMR = .095).

Based on the study by Carré and colleagues (2013), using all items of the BES and a three-factor structure, the model fit was improved, but not completely satisfactory (CFI = .781, RMSEA = .069, SRMR = .073).
text.formatted: Based on the study by <ref type="bibr">Carré and colleagues (2013)</ref>, using all items of the BES and a three-factor structure, the model fit was improved, but not completely satisfactory (CFI = .781, RMSEA = .069, SRMR = .073).

text.text: Because this model was superior to the 2-factor model, we used the 3-factor model as a basis and pruned items that showed weaker loadings.

We used an iterative approach, where we omitted the weakest loading item, checked the model fit, and omitted the next weakest loading item until we reached a satisfactory model fit including CFI > .90.
text.formatted: We used an iterative approach, where we omitted the weakest loading item, checked the model fit, and omitted the next weakest loading item until we reached a satisfactory model fit including CFI > .90.

text.text: All model fits and factor loadings of these iterative models are described in the Supplemental Table 7.
text.formatted: All model fits and factor loadings of these iterative models are described in the Supplemental Table <ref type="table">7</ref>.

text.text: Two items were omitted for emotional disconnection and three for cognitive empathy.
The reliability of these factors was w = .81 for emotional contagion (6 items), w = .72 for emotional disconnection (4 items), and w = .72 for cognitive empathy (5 items).
Using this pruned three-factor solution was not feasible to include into our main analyses for multiple reasons.
First, the third factor (Disconnection) is a method factor which only included negatively worded items.
Furthermore, an exploratory factor analysis also yielded only two factors based on an Eigenvalue of 1 (see Supplemental Figure 1), casting doubt on the added value of a third factor.
text.formatted: Furthermore, an exploratory factor analysis also yielded only two factors based on an Eigenvalue of 1 (see Supplemental Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>), casting doubt on the added value of a third factor.

text.text: Second, the present study will be better comparable to the large body of previous empathy research if we stay within the two-factor framework.
Third, the pruned threefactor solution will be even less comparable to previous research, given that items were omitted, which limits the comparability of the present findings.
Thus, we decided to treat empathy, as well as its emotional and cognitive facets, as manifest predictors of the levels and trajectories of well-being and health.
